lines.text: If you flew a spacecraft straight into the Sun, how far in could it really go, and how much of what is down there has anyone actually measured?
Here's the strange part. One spacecraft has already flown through the Sun's atmosphere, and it came out working. The gas around it was hundreds of times hotter than the Sun's surface.
Behind its shield, the instruments sat at room temperature.
And the trip there is the real villain. It takes fifty-five times more energy to reach the Sun than to reach Mars. Why? We'll go in stage by stage, and watch Tick's stamp turn from measured to model.
The real spacecraft is called Parker Solar Probe. It's the fastest thing humans have ever built. It's the closest we've come, so it's our guide. Everything it measured gets a green stamp.
Everything past it gets a different one.
First, the problem with falling.
You'd think the Sun would be the easiest target there is. Everything in the solar system is falling around it. But Earth isn't sitting still.
It's moving sideways around the Sun at twenty-nine point eight kilometres every second.
Anything launched from Earth starts with that sideways speed. NASA's figure is sixty-seven thousand miles an hour. Aim straight at the Sun, and you miss. You go around it, like Earth does.

To leave the solar system entirely, you need about twelve point three kilometres a second more. To fall in, you must take away all twenty-nine point eight. Dropping in is more than twice as hard as flying out.
That's why NASA picked one of the most powerful rockets there is.

Here's the sum. At Earth's distance, escaping the Sun needs a speed of about forty-two point one kilometres a second. Earth already supplies twenty-nine point eight of it. There's no such head start for falling in.
Every kilometre a second of sideways speed has to be paid back.
If you could somehow stop that sideways motion, the fall would take about sixty-five days. You'd arrive at about six hundred and sixteen kilometres a second. That's almost the Sun's escape speed.
But a straight drop of a hundred and forty-nine point six million kilometres isn't how anyone gets there. The real trip is years of looping.
Parker Solar Probe launched in August 2018 on one of the most powerful rockets in the world. NASA called a strong launch only a good start on shedding that sideways speed.

So it used Venus. A normal gravity assist speeds a spacecraft up. Parker's seven flybys did the opposite: they slowed it down, so each orbit dipped closer to the Sun. NASA called the first one a handbrake turn.
The seven dates were October 2018, December 2019, July 2020, February 2021, October 2021, August 2023, and November 2024. Each one lowered the lowest point of the next orbit.

The second flyby alone took away two point nine kilometres a second. The last, in November 2024, set up the closest pass yet. By then the probe had been looping for six years, over a plan of twenty-four orbits.
On the twenty-fourth of December, 2024, it passed within six point one six million kilometres of the Sun's surface. It was moving at one hundred and ninety-one kilometres a second.
That's about six times Earth's own speed. NASA says that's fast enough to cross from New York to Tokyo in under a minute.
Two days later, a beacon signal told Earth the probe was fine. In September 2025, it flew the same distance again, at the same speed.
In solar radii, that pass was nine point eight six, measured from the Sun's centre. That's under five percent of the Earth to Sun distance.
The corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere, and it's a strange place. NASA says it gets hotter the farther it stretches from the surface.

But Parker had already crossed the Sun's edge years earlier. On the twenty-eighth of April, 2021, on its eighth pass, it went through a boundary called the Alfvén surface. That was at eighteen point eight solar radii.
NASA called it the first time a spacecraft had touched the Sun.
NASA described it as the end of the solar atmosphere and the beginning of the solar wind. And it isn't a smooth shell. NASA reported spikes and valleys in it.

And even at its closest, Parker was still far above the surface. Six point one six million kilometres is nearly nine Sun-radii. The Sun's own radius is six hundred and ninety-five thousand seven hundred kilometres.
Now the mystery. The Sun's visible surface is about five and a half thousand degrees Celsius. But the corona above it reaches two million. That's hundreds of times hotter. Nobody knows why.
NASA calls it one of the greatest unanswered questions in astrophysics. And heat can't just flow from a cooler place to a hotter one, so the surface can't simply be warming the corona.
If you looked at temperature alone, the probe would look doomed. NASA hoped that measuring from inside the corona would help solve the heating puzzle.
So why isn't the probe melting? Because temperature and heat aren't the same. Temperature measures how fast the particles are moving. Heat is the total energy they pass on.

NASA's comparison is a hand in a hot oven versus a hand in boiling water. In the thin air of the oven, your hand doesn't get nearly as hot as in the denser water. The corona is like that, only far thinner.
At its base, there are about a million billion particles in every cubic metre. At the surface there are around a hundred million times as many.
The shield does the rest. It's two sheets of carbon with a carbon foam core, eleven point four centimetres thick. Its sunward face can reach nearly fourteen hundred degrees Celsius.
On the December 2024 pass, NASA expected it to warm to about eighteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit, which is nearly a thousand Celsius. Behind it, the instruments stay near thirty.
The panels that power the probe fold back behind the shield, and the small edge left in the light is still enough to risk overheating. So the whole craft is built to hide.
Everything up to here was read off a real thermometer, aboard a real probe. This is where the stamp changes.
Below the probe's closest pass, the Sun has no flat floor to land on. It's a ball of plasma. What we call the surface is the photosphere, the layer we see from Earth.

It's only a few hundred kilometres thick, and it's about five and a half thousand degrees. The gas there is about ten thousand times thinner than the air we breathe. That's why a spacecraft can't land.
There's nothing to land on. Averaged over the whole Sun, the density is about fourteen hundred kilograms in every cubic metre. That's heavier than water, for a ball of gas.
Above it sits the chromosphere, about two thousand kilometres thick. It warms to tens of thousands of degrees at its top, and sources disagree on the number.
Above that, the temperature must leap from tens of thousands of degrees to millions. Every number in this stage comes from light collected from far away, and not from a thermometer that went there.
Going in, the first layer is the convection zone. It's about two hundred thousand kilometres deep. Its base sits at seven tenths of the Sun's radius, measured from the centre.
NASA puts its temperature at the bottom around two million degrees.
Hot gas rises, cools at the top, and sinks again. That's how this layer moves energy.
How do we know? The Sun rings like a bell. The waves bounce through it. By studying them, we can locate the bottom of this layer from outside. That's called helioseismology.
Below that is the radiative zone, from about a quarter of the radius out to seven tenths. Here the energy has to crawl. Light bounces from atom to atom.
NASA says it takes about a hundred and seventy thousand years to get to the top of the convection zone. Other estimates put it as low as ten thousand years.
For comparison, the light from the surface reaches Earth in eight minutes and nineteen seconds. So the sunlight on your window this morning spent most of its life getting out.
Notice the arc of the temperature. From the core it falls from fifteen million degrees to five and a half thousand at the surface. Then it climbs again, to two million, in the corona.
At the middle is the core. It reaches out to about a fifth of the Sun's radius, roughly a hundred and thirty-eight thousand kilometres from the centre. That's more than ten Earths, laid end to end.
Its temperature tops fifteen million degrees Celsius. The pressure at the centre is about two hundred and fifty billion times the air pressure at sea level.

Hydrogen is fused into helium here, and that is where the Sun's heat and light begin. Its density is about a hundred and fifty grams per cubic centimetre. That's about eight times the density of lead.
We can't send a probe there, and we can't see it with light. But the core makes ghostly particles called neutrinos. Most go straight out through the Sun.
The count of one kind lets us check the core's temperature in a model, to within about one percent.

scenes.name: What we measured, and what we modelled

lines.text: Let's be honest about where the data ends. From the Sun's surface to its centre is about seven hundred thousand kilometres. A probe has travelled none of it.
Parker is the closest anything we've built has ever been. Down to nine point eight six solar radii, the probe's own instruments sent back real readings.
For the photosphere and chromosphere, we have light, taken from far away.
For the layers inside, we have sound waves and a model of a ball of gas. Even the sound waves can't see the core well, because they mostly feel the outer layers.
And the core's temperature comes from a model, tested against neutrinos. Where the sources disagree, we've said so.
NASA's pages give Parker's top speed as six hundred and ninety-two thousand kilometres an hour in one place, and about six hundred and eighty-seven thousand in another.
The shield's hottest face is quoted as twenty-five hundred degrees Fahrenheit in one place, and eighteen hundred in another.
The photosphere's thickness is quoted as two hundred and fifty miles by one NASA page, and five hundred kilometres by another.
And the top of the chromosphere, ten, twenty or thirty thousand degrees, depending on who you ask.
So here is how to read the stamps. Green means an instrument was there. Blue means light that travelled from far away. Grey means a model, checked against something we can measure.
Even the Alfvén crossing has two descriptions. NASA's page gives it as eighteen point eight radii, and as eight point one million miles above the surface.
Those match only if the miles are counted from the Sun's centre, so we use the radii.
And Parker's own future isn't settled. In September 2025, NASA said the next steps for the mission were under review.
So here's the honest answer. A probe can fly into the Sun's atmosphere. It has, and it kept its instruments at room temperature, because the corona is hot but thin.
It could do that only after seven Venus flybys helped shed much of the speed that Earth gave it. Past that, nobody has gone.
The surface is seen by light, the layers below it by sound waves, and the core by a model that neutrinos check. Every number we gave you for those stages is our best reading from outside.
The Sun was the hard place to reach. Next, we turn around and go the other way.
